description: A security program protects only what it has declared to cover, so a scope that drifts leaves gaps nobody owns. A written scope signed by leadership tells staff, customers and auditors what is inside the boundary and why anything is left out. A short map of how the management processes connect shows the program runs as one system.
implementation_guidance:
Write a scope statement that names the products, services, cloud environments, data centers and other sites, offices, teams, systems and data the security program covers, and explain where the boundary sits with reference to the internal and external factors and the requirements of interested parties.
State what is left out and why, list the suppliers, group entities and interfaces the services in scope depend on, such as the cloud or hosting provider and outsourced operations, and keep a data flow diagram showing where sensitive data, such as payment card data, crosses the boundary.
Have leadership approve the scope in writing, make it available to staff, customers and auditors who need it, and review it at least annually and whenever products, sites, suppliers or customer commitments change.
Describe the main management processes, such as risk assessment, internal audit, management review and corrective action, and how each one feeds the next.
name: ISMS scope and boundaries

evidence.name: Scope statement approved by leadership
evidence.what: ISMS scope statement
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Products, teams, sites, systems and suppliers in scope, what is out and why, and leadership approval with date.

evidence.name: Map of the management processes and how they connect
evidence.what: Map of management processes
evidence.where: A diagram or table in the shared drive.
evidence.shows: Each management process such as risk, audit and review, its owner, and its inputs and outputs.

evidence.name: Scope review after changes to products, sites or suppliers
evidence.what: Scope review after a change
evidence.where: A dated note or new document version after a new product, site or supplier.
evidence.shows: The change, date, whether scope changed, and approval.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no product, site or supplier change happened in [period].

description: Security effort aimed at last year's picture misses the pressures that matter now. A written view of the external and internal factors that shape the program, such as regulation, customer demands, technology change, staffing and funding, keeps risk work and objectives pointed at what actually affects the business.
implementation_guidance:
List the external factors that affect the security program, such as laws and regulators, customer expectations, threat trends, supplier changes and market conditions, and record whether climate change is relevant, for example through its effect on sites, hosting regions, suppliers or customer demands, with the reason either way.
List the internal factors, such as strategy, growth plans, team capacity, technology choices, culture and budget.
Name an owner, and review the list at least annually and after major events such as a funding round, an acquisition, a new market, a new regulation or a serious incident.
Use the list as an input to the risk assessment, the objectives and the scope, and record where a factor led to an action or a decision.
name: Internal and external factors register

evidence.name: Register of external and internal factors
evidence.what: Internal and external factors register
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Factors such as market, law, customers, technology, staff and funding, and how each affects security.

evidence.name: Yearly review notes and decisions taken
evidence.what: Annual review of the factors register
evidence.where: Leadership meeting notes or a dated document version.
evidence.shows: Date, who reviewed, factors added or changed, and decisions taken.

description: Customers, regulators, employees, suppliers and owners each expect something from the security program, and an expectation nobody wrote down is missed until a complaint or an audit finds it. A register of who they are and what each requires shows which expectations the program meets and feeds the obligations register.
implementation_guidance:
List the parties with a stake in security, such as customers, regulators, employees, suppliers, investors and insurers.
Record what each party requires or expects, separating legal, contractual and other expectations, including any that relate to climate change, and note where each came from.
Decide which of those requirements the program will take on, and carry the legal and contractual ones into the compliance obligations register with a named owner.
Review the list at least annually and whenever a major customer, regulator or contract changes.
name: Interested parties and their requirements

evidence.name: Register of interested parties and what each requires
evidence.what: Interested parties register
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Each party such as customers, staff, regulators, investors and suppliers, and what each requires on security.

evidence.name: Review record covering new contracts and regulatory changes
evidence.what: Annual review of interested party requirements
evidence.where: A dated note or document version.
evidence.shows: Date, new contracts and regulatory changes checked, and the changes made.

description: Security work without targets cannot show whether it is succeeding or whether the people and budget behind it are enough. Objectives with an owner, a date and a measure turn intent into something leadership can check, and they show that resources were considered rather than assumed.
implementation_guidance:
Each year, set a small number of security objectives that follow from the security policy, the risk assessment and customer commitments, each worded so it can be measured.
Give every objective an owner, a target, a due date and the people, time and budget needed to reach it.
Define the measures behind each objective: what is measured, how, how often and who reviews the numbers.
Share the objectives with the people who work toward them, review results at management review, record the decisions taken on resources, and update or retire objectives that no longer fit.
name: Security objectives, plans and measures

evidence.name: Security objectives with owners, targets and due dates
evidence.what: Security objectives
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per objective with its target.
evidence.shows: Each objective with its measure, target, owner and due date.

evidence.name: Measures and results compared with targets
evidence.what: Quarterly results compared with security objectives
evidence.where: A dashboard or sheet reviewed at the management review.
evidence.shows: Each objective, target, actual result, and actions where it is off track.

evidence.name: Resourcing decisions for the security program
evidence.what: Security budget and staffing decisions
evidence.where: Leadership minutes or the budget sheet.
evidence.shows: Date, the people, tools and budget approved for security, and requests turned down with the reason.

description: Which controls you run and which you leave out are decisions that customers and auditors will ask you to defend. The statement of applicability records, for every control in the reference set, whether it applies, whether it is in place and why, so each choice traces back to a risk or an obligation rather than habit.
implementation_guidance:
List every control in the reference set you work to, plus any further controls you chose from other sources such as regulations or contracts, and record for each whether it applies, whether it is in place and who owns it.
Give a reason for every control you include and every one you leave out, pointing to a risk, a legal or contractual requirement or the scope, not a general statement.
Mark controls that a supplier performs for you as inherited, and attach the supplier's report or certificate as support.
Have risk owners and leadership approve each version, keep every approved version, review the statement at least annually, and reissue it when risk treatment or scope changes.
name: Statement of Applicability

evidence.name: Statement of Applicability showing every decision and reason
evidence.what: Statement of Applicability
evidence.where: Controls module, built from the applicability decision on each control.
evidence.shows: Every Annex A control, included or not, the reason, and its implementation status.

evidence.name: Approval of each version by risk owners and leadership
evidence.what: Approval of each Statement of Applicability version
evidence.where: Email, signed note or minutes from risk owners and leadership.
evidence.shows: Version, date, approvers, and what changed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that the Statement of Applicability did not change in [period].

evidence.name: Supplier certificates behind inherited controls
evidence.what: Supplier certificates for inherited controls
evidence.where: Vendors module, with certificates attached to each supplier.
evidence.shows: Supplier, certificate type, scope, expiry date, and the controls inherited.

description: A policy nobody can find, or one that exists in three conflicting versions, does more harm than no policy because people follow the wrong one. Controlled documents carry an owner, a version, an approval and a review date, and they sit where the right people can read them and the wrong people cannot change them.
implementation_guidance:
List the documents and records the security program needs, including every one that the standards, laws and contracts you work to require and the operating procedures staff follow to run the systems in scope, and name an owner for each.
Give every document a title, version, date, owner and next review date, at least yearly for policies and procedures, keep it in an agreed format, and require a named approver to review it before it is published or changed.
Keep documents in a controlled system of record with access set by role, backup and version history, withdraw superseded versions from use, and protect paper records the same way where they exist.
Set retention and disposal rules for records that meet legal and contractual periods, and identify and control documents from outside sources that the program relies on, such as supplier reports and regulator notices.
name: Document and record management

evidence.name: Document control procedure covering approval, versions and retention
evidence.what: Document control procedure
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: How documents are written, approved, versioned, shared, kept and retired.

evidence.name: Version history and approval record for each document
evidence.what: Version history and approvals for each document
evidence.where: Documents module version history.
evidence.shows: Each version with date, author, approver and a summary of the change.

evidence.name: Access and retention settings for the document store
evidence.what: Document store access and retention settings
evidence.where: Screenshot or export of sharing and retention settings in the shared drive or Documents module.
evidence.shows: Who can read and edit, the retention period, and deletion rules.

description: Security work that nobody scheduled happens only when someone remembers it. An operating plan lists the recurring activities that keep the management system running, such as risk assessment, access reviews, audits, management review and training, with an owner, a due date and the standard each must meet.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an operating plan that lists each recurring security activity with its owner, schedule and expected output, and review the plan at least annually.
Define what counts as done for each activity, such as the scope, the method, the approver and the record it must leave.
Before changing the management system or the services in scope, record the reason, the expected effect, the owner, the timing and the resources needed, and after any unplanned change, review its effect and act on any harm it caused.
List the security work that suppliers, contractors or other group entities do on your behalf, set the standard they must meet in the contract or service agreement, and check it at the supplier review.
name: Security operating plan

evidence.name: Operating plan listing activities, owners and schedule
evidence.what: Security operating plan
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: A yearly calendar of security activities such as reviews, tests, training and audits, each with owner and date.

evidence.name: Records showing planned activities were completed
evidence.what: Quarterly check that planned activities were done
evidence.where: The operating plan with status marked, and a link to each record.

evidence.shows: The change or supplier, date, the security risks considered, and approval.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no major changes or new outsourcing happened in [period].

description: A management system that only maintains itself slowly goes stale. Collecting improvement ideas from audits, incidents, measures and staff, deciding which to act on and tracking them to completion is how the program improves each year instead of repeating itself.
implementation_guidance:
Keep one improvement log that takes input from audits, incidents, measurement results, management review, customer feedback and staff suggestions.
Assess each item for benefit and effort, decide whether to act, and record the decision and the reason.
Give accepted items an owner and a due date, track them as tasks, and close them only with evidence that the change was made.
Check a sample of completed improvements at management review to confirm they had the intended effect.

evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: How anyone raises an improvement, who decides, and how it is tracked.

evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per improvement.
evidence.shows: Each improvement with source, owner, decision, due date and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no improvements were raised in [period].

evidence.what: Annual review of improvements and their effect
evidence.where: Management review minutes or a dated note.
evidence.shows: Each completed improvement, whether it worked, and any follow up.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no improvements were completed in [period].

description: The people who run security, such as the security lead, administrators, incident responders and internal auditors, need skills well beyond general awareness. Recording what each role requires, what each holder has and how gaps were closed shows that the work is done by people able to do it.
implementation_guidance:
List the roles that carry security duties, such as security lead, system and database administrators, on call responders, internal auditors, risk owners and, where they exist, key custodians.
Define the skills, experience and qualifications each role needs, building on the job description.
Before someone takes up a security role and at least once a year after, record what they can show, such as training, certificates, past experience or a practical assessment, and note any gaps.
Close gaps with training, mentoring, supervision or a change of assignment, set a date for each action, and check afterwards that it worked.
name: Competence of people in security roles

evidence.what: Competence requirements for security roles

evidence.shows: Skills, knowledge, experience or certifications needed for each security role.

evidence.name: Competence record for each person in a security role
evidence.what: Competence record for each person in a security role
evidence.where: CV, certificates and training records, kept in the HR tool.
evidence.shows: Person, role, how they meet each requirement, and any gaps found.

evidence.name: Training or other actions taken to close gaps
evidence.what: Actions taken to close competence gaps
evidence.where: Training records, course certificates or mentoring plans.

evidence.if_none: A dated note that no competence gaps were found in [period].

description: Security messages reach the right people only when someone decided in advance what to say, when, to whom and through which channel. A communication plan covers routine messages and urgent ones, so staff, customers, suppliers and authorities hear what they need without anyone improvising.
implementation_guidance:
List the security topics that need communicating, such as policy changes, incidents, threats, audit results and customer commitments.
State the audience, the timing or trigger, the channel and the sender for each topic.
Cover internal messages to staff and leadership as well as external ones to customers, suppliers, regulators and the public.
Review the plan at least annually, and check that messages were sent and understood, for example through acknowledgments or feedback.
name: Security communication plan

evidence.name: Security communication plan
evidence.what: Security communication plan
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: What is communicated, to whom, when, by whom and through which channel.

evidence.name: List of all security messages sent under the plan in the period, with date, audience, channel and topic. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of security messages sent in the period
evidence.where: Slack or email messages, newsletters and all hands slides.
evidence.shows: Every message in the period with date, audience, channel and topic.

description: During an incident, searching for the right regulator, law enforcement contact or provider escalation path wastes time you do not have. A current contact list and a few active community memberships bring help and early warning faster, and they stop individuals from improvising disclosures.
implementation_guidance:
List the authorities you may need to contact, such as data protection regulators, sector or financial supervisors, national cyber agencies or CERTs, law enforcement, and emergency services for any site you run, with contact details, the situations that call for contact and any legal reporting deadline.
Name an owner for the list and who may contact each authority, require the incident lead and legal counsel to agree before a regulator or law enforcement is contacted about a security incident, except where life or safety is at risk, and log each contact made with its date, reason and outcome.
Join the security communities, information sharing groups and professional bodies that match your technology and sector, such as a sector ISAC or a national CERT service, and name a person who follows each one and passes on what matters.
Check the list and memberships at least annually and after a change of regulator, jurisdiction or site, and confirm each contact channel still works, recording the date and result.
name: Contacts with authorities and security communities

evidence.name: Contact list for authorities and security communities
evidence.what: Contact list for authorities and security groups
evidence.where: A page in the incident runbook.
evidence.shows: Police cyber unit, data protection regulator, national CERT and cloud provider support, with contact details.

evidence.name: Memberships or subscriptions to security communities
evidence.what: Security community memberships and subscriptions
evidence.where: Receipts, sign up emails, or a list of feeds followed.
evidence.shows: Each group or feed, such as a CERT advisory list or vendor security bulletin, and who follows it.

evidence.name: Yearly check that contact details still work
evidence.what: Annual check of the contact list
evidence.where: A dated note or document version.
evidence.shows: Date, who checked, and each contact confirmed or updated.

description: Attackers change tools faster than a yearly assessment can follow, so learning about a new technique only after an incident means learning too late. Collecting reports on threats to your stack, checking them against what you run and acting on the ones that matter turns outside news into earlier fixes and better detection.
implementation_guidance:
Choose sources that fit your technology and sector, such as vendor security bulletins, cloud provider notices, government and national CERT alerts, known exploited vulnerability lists, sector sharing groups such as an ISAC, and trusted research, and record why each was chosen.
Name a person or team to read the sources on a written schedule, at least weekly, and to assess urgent alerts, such as an actively exploited flaw in software you run, on the day they arrive, judging which items affect your systems, data or suppliers.
Record each relevant item with its assessment and the action taken, such as a patch, a detection rule, a configuration change, a supplier question or a note to staff, with an owner and a date.
Feed confirmed threats into the risk assessment, vulnerability priorities and incident planning, give leadership a summary of threat trends at each management review, and review the choice of sources at least annually.
name: Threat source monitoring

evidence.what: Threat sources and review routine
evidence.where: A short document or runbook section.
evidence.shows: Feeds followed such as the CISA known exploited list and vendor advisories, who reads them, and how often.

evidence.name: Log of threats reviewed and actions taken
evidence.what: Threat review log
evidence.where: A sheet, a Slack channel or tickets.
evidence.shows: Date, threat, whether it affects us, the action and owner.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no relevant threats were found in [period], with the sources checked.

evidence.shows: Each finding with date published, date found in our systems, date fixed, and days taken.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no known exploited vulnerability affected our systems in [period].

description: Many tasks need data that looks real without being real, such as support screens, analytics, demos, training and test environments. Masking or pseudonymizing sensitive fields limits what a leaked export, a curious employee or a contractor can see while the work carries on.
implementation_guidance:
Use the data classification to list the fields that need masking, such as personal identifiers, contact details, account and card numbers, and credentials, and check the list against the privacy, sector and payment card rules that apply.
Choose a method for each use, such as redaction, partial display, tokenization, hashing or synthetic replacement, and keep the masking rules in reviewed code or configuration so every change is approved and recorded.
Apply masking by default in support tools, analytics exports, logs, demos and lower environments, allow unmasked access only to approved roles, and show no more than the issuer prefix and the last four digits of a card number to anyone whose role does not need the full number.
At least annually and whenever schemas or data types change, test that masked data cannot be reversed by combining fields or reading a mapping, and record the result.

evidence.what: Masking standard
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Each sensitive field, its masking method, and where masking applies, such as test, support and analytics.

evidence.name: List of all data sets used for test, support or analytics in the period, with owner, masking method and date checked. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: Data sets used for test, support or analytics, with masking method
evidence.where: Test databases, support tools and analytics exports.
evidence.shows: Every such data set in the period, its owner, the masking method, and a screenshot of masked fields.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no data was copied for test, support or analytics use in [period].

description: Sensitive data usually leaves by ordinary routes such as email, file sharing, chat, personal cloud storage, removable media and open storage buckets. Setting rules for those routes and watching them for bulk or unusual transfers lets you stop or catch a leak that no attacker needed to break in to cause.
implementation_guidance:
List the routes data can leave by, such as email, file sharing, chat, code repositories, storage buckets, removable media, printing and screenshots, for the systems that hold confidential or restricted data.
Set rules that fit the data classification, such as blocking external sharing of restricted data, limiting downloads and forwarding, and warning before a risky action.
Turn on the sharing controls and leakage alerts in the email, file, chat, endpoint, network egress and cloud storage tools you use, including alerts for bulk downloads and public links, block or restrict removable storage on company devices through device management, allowing only encrypted media by approved exception, and keep a record of the settings.
Triage leakage alerts within a set time, such as one business day, through the security event process, raise confirmed leaks as incidents, and review exceptions and rule tuning at least quarterly, recording the outcome of each, so people can work without bypassing the rules.
name: Outbound data leak controls

evidence.name: Leakage prevention and sharing settings in email, chat and file tools
evidence.what: Data sharing and leak prevention settings
evidence.where: Admin settings screenshots from Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, Slack and file tools.
evidence.shows: External sharing limits, data loss prevention rules, and who can change them.

evidence.name: Alerts and exceptions that were reviewed and followed up
evidence.what: Data leak alerts and exceptions reviewed
evidence.where: Data loss prevention alerts or sharing reports from the admin console, with review notes.
evidence.shows: Each alert or exception with date, user, file, decision and follow up.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no data leak alerts or exceptions in [period]", with the empty report.

description: Logs from different systems line up into one timeline only if their clocks agree. Drifting clocks break incident reconstruction, weaken audit trails and can cause failures in certificate and token checks, so every system should take its time from a small set of trusted sources.
implementation_guidance:
Choose trusted time sources, such as the cloud provider's time service or at least two internal time servers that take time from national or satellite references, and record them.
Configure servers, containers, network devices, databases and managed services to take time only from those sources, restrict who can change time settings, and log every change to them.
Record log timestamps in one standard time zone, normally UTC, or with an explicit offset, so events from every source can be compared directly.
Set the largest clock offset allowed, for example one second, alert when a system exceeds it, check a sample of systems at least quarterly, and confirm the setting whenever a new image, device or account is built.
name: Time synchronization

evidence.name: Trusted time sources and how systems use them
evidence.what: Time source standard
evidence.where: A short engineering note or runbook section.
evidence.shows: The time source used, such as the cloud provider time service, and how servers and services use it.

evidence.name: List of all in scope systems in the period, with time source, measured clock offset and date checked. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of systems with clock check results
evidence.where: A command or monitoring view that shows clock offset on each system.
evidence.shows: Every in scope system, its time source, the offset found and the date checked.

description: Staff browse from the same devices that hold credentials and customer data, and one click on a malicious or deceptive site can hand an attacker both. Blocking known bad categories and risky downloads, and logging what was blocked, cuts exposure to malware and phishing without relying on every user to spot every trap.
implementation_guidance:
Define which website categories are blocked or restricted on company devices, such as malware, phishing, newly registered domains and unapproved file sharing, and record them in the filtering standard.
Apply the filter to every managed device whether the user is in the office or remote, through device management, DNS filtering, a secure web gateway or a proxy, confirm each newly enrolled device is covered, and where servers or administrative workstations handle card data or other high value systems, give them no general web access and allow only the named update and service destinations they need.
Grant exceptions by request with an approver, a reason and an end date, and remove expired exceptions at each review.
Review filter coverage against the device inventory, blocked activity and open exceptions at least quarterly, record the review, and use repeat hits to update training and tighten the rules.
name: Harmful website blocking

evidence.name: Web filtering standard covering blocked categories and exceptions
evidence.what: Web filtering standard
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Blocked categories such as malware and phishing sites, the tool used, and how exceptions are approved.

evidence.name: Report of filter coverage and blocked activity
evidence.what: Web filter coverage and block report
evidence.where: Exported from the filtering tool, such as Cloudflare Gateway, or from the endpoint tool.
evidence.shows: Devices covered compared with the device list, blocked requests, and exceptions.

description: Server rooms, comms cabinets and data centers that you run yourself rely on power, cooling, cabling and hardware that a fire, a flood, a power cut or a careless repair can take down or expose. Where no cloud provider carries that duty for you, assessing the hazards at each site, fitting protections to match and keeping service records is what keeps systems running and data safe.
implementation_guidance:
List each site you run that holds equipment or information, such as an office comms cabinet, a server room, a data center or a recovery site, name an owner for each, and assess its hazards, such as fire, flood, heat, power loss and tampering, at least annually and after any change to the site.
Fit protections that match the hazards, such as fire detection and suppression, water detection, locked racks kept away from windows and public view, uninterruptible power with a generator or a tested shutdown, monitored cooling, and cabling in protected routes with power and network kept apart.
Service site equipment and protections at the intervals the manufacturer or the building sets, using only approved engineers, supervise their work in secure areas, remove or wipe storage from any equipment, including laptops, before it leaves for repair, keep a record of each fault and service visit, and where you run card terminals, ATMs or other payment devices, keep a list of each device and its location, inspect them for tampering or substitution on a schedule set by risk, and train staff at those sites to spot and report tampering.
Test power failover, alarms and suppression at least annually and follow up every failed test; where the only site is a shared office in a managed building, keep the landlord's fire, power and maintenance certificates instead of duplicating them.
name: Environmental and equipment protection at own sites
